# Seismic waves

<!-- foundations -->
```dataviewjs
dv.view("_dv/foundations")
```
<!-- /foundations -->

## summary

**Seismic waves** are packets of elastic strain energy that propagate through the interior and across the surface of the [[earth]], most commonly generated by the abrupt rupture of a geological [[fault]] during an [[earthquake]]. First systematically recorded and analyzed in the late nineteenth century, these acoustic vibrations travel at speeds governed by the density and elastic moduli of the rock strata they traverse. In geophysics and global hazard assessment, they provide both the primary mechanism of catastrophic structural destruction and the indispensable diagnostic probe used to reconstruct the layered internal structure of terrestrial planets.

## you gotta know

- Categorized broadly into body waves, which travel through the planetary interior, and surface waves, which propagate along the planetary crust; body waves are further subdivided into primary compressional waves and secondary shear waves.
- *P-waves* are longitudinal waves that compress and dilate rock parallel to the direction of propagation, traveling fastest among all seismic disturbances and uniquely capable of moving through solids, liquids, and gases because fluid media possess volume elasticity.
- *S-waves* are transverse shear waves that displace particles perpendicular to wave motion and cannot penetrate liquids or gases because fluids lack shear strength, a physical constraint that creates an extensive *shadow zone* revealing the fluid nature of the outer core.
- Surface waves, divided into horizontally polarizing *Love waves* and retrograde elliptical *Rayleigh waves*, travel slower than body waves but exhibit much lower geometric attenuation, making them responsible for the vast majority of architectural destruction during an [[earthquake]].
- Seismograph networks determine the epicenter of an event by calculating the travel-time differential between the arrival of the fast *P-waves* and slower *S-waves*, requiring recordings from a minimum of three distinct geographical monitoring stations to achieve spatial triangulation.
- Discontinuities in wave velocity mapped planetary boundaries, notably the crust-mantle boundary discovered by *Andrija Mohorovičić*, the core-mantle boundary identified by *Beno Gutenberg*, and the solid inner core identified by *Inge Lehmann* through faint *P-wave* reflections within the core shadow.
- Extremely large seismic events can excite planetary free oscillations, or normal modes, causing the entire globe to ring like a bell at discrete low-frequency eigenperiods, an acoustic phenomenon first definitively recorded following the massive 1960 Valdivia temblor.

## connections

- [[earthquake]] — the sudden fracture and slip of crustal rocks that radiates stored elastic potential energy outward as destructive mechanical waves.
- [[plate-tectonics]] — the overarching convective mechanism whose continuous plate collisions and subduction zones supply the tectonic strain driving wave generation.
- [[fault]] — the physical fracture surface along which localized displacement initiates the high-frequency slip pulse that launches wave trains.
- [[richter-scale]] — the historical empirical calibration based on the peak amplitude recorded by a *Wood-Anderson* seismograph on a [[logarithmic-scale]].
- [[moment-magnitude-scale]] — the modern seismological standard estimating total energy directly from fault rupture area and slip rather than recorded wave amplitude.
- [[earth]] — the planetary body whose concentric internal layers were deciphered almost entirely by tracking the refraction and reflection of internal wave paths.
- [[volcano]] — the magmatic system whose underground fluid transport generates distinctive long-period volcanic tremors and high-frequency tectonic swarms.
- [[industrial-revolution]] — the historical era whose rapid development of precision instrumentation and electrical telegraphy enabled coordinated, multi-station seismic recording.
